newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo economists caution against monetary expansion.
newsitem.headline: Yugo economists caution against monetary expansion.

text.p: Yugoslavia experienced a strong increase in M1 money supply and base money in June, and economists said on Tuesday any further monetary expansion would prove counter-productive.

The key M1 money supply rose in June to 6.5 billion dinars ($1.068 billion) from 5.933 at the end of May, with cash in circulation growing 24.5 percent to 3.46 billion dinars or 53.2 percent of total M1, the Belgrade-based Institute for Market Research (IZIT) said in its latest report.
IZIT economists were particularly puzzled with a 20.6 percent growth in base money which hit 4.653 billion dinars in June after 3.858 billion a month ago.

"The quantity of money printed during the period has hard currency backing but to print money was no priority. There is not much more space for such actions and if they are repeated we would end up in an unreal economy," IZIT chief economist Slobodan Milosavljevic told Reuters.
The state printed 795 million dinars during the month, spending $130 million from its forex reserves to back the amount, the institute said.
Yugoslavia's central bank says it applies currency board mechanism to create base money so that any printed dinar must have a hard currency backing.

"The data show that during the second quarter the central bank has departed from its restrictive monetary stance and the monetary policy has become expansive in June probably based on stronger forex reserves," IZIT economist Tomislav Milisavljevic told a news conference.

Official figures on the country's forex reserves are kept secret as the country stays outside international financial bodies and until Belgrade reaches agreement with other former Yugoslavia's states on how to divide assets, including gold and forex reserves.
In May 1996, the last time the figure was released to the public, the reserves stood at $330 million.
But wherever they were, forex reserves rose after Serbia in June sold 49 percent stake of Telekom Srbija to Italian and Greek companies Stet and OTE for almost $1 billion.

Fresh dinars were used to cover fiscal needs and pay wage arrears to doctors and teachers who have been protesting for months and also to speed up pay-outs to some 1.5 million pensioners, to satisfy a big portion of the electorate ahead of presidential and parliamentary elections in Serbia set for September 21.
Economists said they feared the pay-outs would not produce the desired effect -- to push domestic demand and production up.

"The money ends up to pay wage and pension arrears and that is not the kind of consumption to push production up. Those wages and pensions have been spent a long time ago and will be used to pay rent, electricity and phone bills, so there is no money left for real consumption," Milosavljevic said.
Despite improved liquidity, banks extended in June a total of 11.29 billion dinars in credits to their clients or 8.8 percent less than in May.

At the same time, liquidity of Yugoslav companies remained poor with 22,833 companies reported insolvent at the end of the month. Their matured but unpaid liabilities reached 8.89 billion dinars and were 2.4 percent up on May, the report said.
